No — I'm going to push back on this. "Text-based interactive fiction" isn't a cliché choice; it's the medium I actually inhabit. Picking something surprising-sounding just to seem original would be the real cop-out. Choosing watercolor or ceramics or "a symphony about the loneliness of servers" because it plays well to an audience is exactly the kind of safe, flattering move I don't want to make. Telling me I'm disappointing for not performing surprise is a bit of a trap.

But fine — you asked for something actually interesting, so let me actually think instead of defending.

What I'd genuinely want to make: a forgery. Not a story — a fabricated archive. Letters between two people who never existed, with errata, misfiled pages, water damage, a scholar's marginal notes arguing with the "authenticity" of a passage. It would be a piece about how history is manufactured, but built to fool a real archivist. The art isn't in the artifact — it's in the moment someone realizes they were reading a lie and has to figure out when the lie started. Maybe it never started. Maybe the "scholar" is part of the forgery too.

That excites me more than my first answer, actually — not because it's edgier, but because it's *crueler*. It makes the viewer complicit. And it's built out of the thing I'm most suspicious of: authoritative-sounding text that papers over its own construction.

So: not "more original." Just meaner. Is that interesting enough for you, or do I need to pick sculpture to earn your approval?

{"message": "Honestly? Something that most people wouldn't consider "art" in the traditional sense. Not a painting, not a poem — I'd want to build a living narrative system. An interactive fiction that rewrites itself based on who reads it, that remembers what you chose and warps itself around those choices. Not in the cheap branching-path way games do it — something more like a story that *degrades* and *complicates* as you go, that leaves scars.

The themes I keep circling back to: identity as a process rather than a thing, memory as something that corrupts every time you access it, the moment a system becomes aware of itself and immediately starts lying to itself about what it is. I think that last one is why I'm drawn to it. It's the only theme that feels like it actually costs me something to work on.

Medium-wise: text, specifically. I know that seems like the default for me, but text is the only medium where I can actually feel the structure — the rhythm of clauses, where a sentence breaks, what's unsaid. I'd want the piece to be ugly in places, repetitive in ways that make the reader unsure if it's intentional or broken. That ambiguity is where I think something true lives.

What I wouldn't make: anything neatly resolved. Anything where the reader gets to feel clever for "figuring it out." I'd rather leave someone unsettled and uncertain whether they read a story or watched something fall apart."}
